standard_text: Find quotients of rational numbers; understand that if p and q are integers, then -(p/q) = (-p)/q = p/(-q) for all nonzero integers.

progression.narrative:
This standard has two braided demands: a rule about where a negative sign can live in a fraction, and the actual work of dividing rational numbers. The spine is the sign story. A quotient of two signed numbers follows the same rules as a product: same signs give a positive result, different signs give a negative one. That single idea -- division inherits multiplication's sign behavior -- is what the whole standard rests on, so the arc opens by settling it and by settling the identity -(p/q) = (-p)/q = p/(-q): one negative sign can sit in front of the fraction, on top, or on the bottom, and the value is the same. The trap is a second negative sign, because two negatives cancel back to positive.

From the sign rule the standard builds computation. Students first find the quotient of two signed integers -- divide the sizes, then attach the sign. Next they calculate a quotient as a decimal by actually dividing numerator by denominator, since a fraction bar means division. Then they divide fractions by multiplying by the reciprocal (keep-change-flip), carrying the sign rule through. With the calculator not allowed, every number stays clean and every quotient is checkable by hand. Students then apply signed division to real situations -- a rate of descent, an average daily change -- where the sign of the quotient carries meaning. The capstone reverses the opening move: generate several equivalent forms of a negative fraction, showing fluent command of where the sign may go. The through-line we keep naming: dividing signed numbers works exactly like multiplying them, and a single negative sign can be written in three equal places.

steps.rationale: The standard's named identity: -(p/q) = (-p)/q = p/(-q). Recognizing that one negative sign can sit in three places -- and that two negatives cancel -- is the sign idea the rest of the division work depends on.

The first computation: find the quotient of two signed integers by dividing the sizes and applying the sign rule (same signs positive, different signs negative), which division inherits from multiplication.
The At-proficiency demand: calculate a quotient as a decimal by dividing numerator by denominator, since a fraction bar means division. The sign is attached after the division.
The difficult band: divide fractions by multiplying by the reciprocal (keep-change-flip), carrying the signed-division rule through the harder number type.
Apply signed division to real contexts -- a rate of descent, an average change -- where the sign of the quotient carries meaning. Bounded to clean rational quotients the spec's number types allow.
The Above-proficiency synthesis: generate multiple equivalent forms of a negative fraction, demonstrating fluent command of the -(p/q) = (-p)/q = p/(-q) identity from the other direction.

skills.name: Recall basic division facts fluently

prerequisite_skill.description: Recall multiplication and division facts through 12 x 12 as inverse operations.

skills.i_do_script: A division fact is a groups question with a picture behind it: 45 / 5 asks 'how many groups of 5 fit in 45?' -- picture 45 dots dealt into rows of 5 and count the rows: 9. That's the same as using the times table backwards: I know 9 x 5 = 45, so 45 / 5 = 9. If I get stuck, I skip-count by the divisor until I reach the dividend. These facts have to be automatic, because every quotient in this standard starts with a plain division fact before I worry about signs.

canonical_error.pattern: Recalls a near-miss fact or reverses the relationship
canonical_error.why: The student grabs a neighboring multiplication fact instead of the exact one. Division asks for the factor that multiplies the divisor to the dividend.

skills.item_template: A single whole-number division fact. Short numeric response fluency bank.

redirect_script.stop: What times the divisor gives the top number?
redirect_script.prompt: Turn it into a multiplication question: 56 / 8 means '8 times what is 56?' Skip-count by 8 if you need to: 8, 16, 24, 32, 40, 48, 56 -- that's 7 jumps.
redirect_script.praise: You used the times table backwards -- that's exactly how division works.

vocabulary.definition: The number being divided (the top number in a fraction bar).
The number you divide by (the bottom number in a fraction bar).
The answer to a division problem.

worked_example_script.text: Show 63 as a bar split into equal groups of 7 -- how many groups fit?
What number times 7 equals 63?
If a student says 8, ask 'what is 8 x 7? Is that 63?'
Your turn: 72 / 8, then 54 / 9.

skills.name: Determine the sign of a product of signed numbers

prerequisite_skill.description: Apply the sign rules for multiplying signed numbers (from 7.NS.3): same signs positive, different signs negative.

skills.i_do_script: The sign rule isn't a decree -- a pattern forces it. Watch: 2 x (-5) = -10, 1 x (-5) = -5, 0 x (-5) = 0. The answers climb by 5 every step, so the next step, (-1) x (-5), has to be +5. Multiplying signed numbers is all about counting negative signs. Same signs make a positive; different signs make a negative. Watch: (-3) x (-4) -- two negatives, so the answer is positive 12. And (-6) x 2 -- one negative, so the answer is negative 12. This matters because division follows the exact same sign rule: division of integers holds the same properties as multiplication.

canonical_error.pattern: Loses track of how many negative signs there are
canonical_error.example: Says (-3) x (-4) = -12 (thinking 'a negative makes it negative') instead of +12
canonical_error.why: The student stops at the first negative sign instead of counting both. Two negatives cancel to a positive; one negative stays negative.

skills.item_template: A product of two signed numbers, or a sign-only judgment. Short numeric response fluency bank.

sample_items.stem: Two negatives multiplied give a ___ answer.

redirect_script.stop: How many negative signs do you see?
redirect_script.prompt: Run the pattern again: when the answers reach zero, do they stop or keep climbing? Count the negatives. An even number (like two) makes the answer positive; an odd number (like one) makes it negative. (-3) x (-4) has two, so it is positive.
redirect_script.praise: You counted the negatives -- that's the whole sign rule.

vocabulary.definition: The result of multiplying numbers together.
Same signs give a positive result; different signs give a negative result.

worked_example_script.text: Look at this pattern: 2 x (-5) = -10, 1 x (-5) = -5, 0 x (-5) = 0 -- the answers climb by 5 each step. Keep it going two more steps: (-1) x (-5) = ? and (-2) x (-5) = ?
How many negative signs are in each? Same or different signs?
(-5) x (-2): two negatives -> positive 10. (-5) x 2: one negative -> negative 10.
If a student writes (-5) x (-2) = -10, ask 'do two negatives stay negative or flip to positive?'
Your turn: (-8) x (-1), then 4 x (-6).

skills.name: Identify equivalent forms of a negative fraction
skills.i_do_script: A fraction bar is a division, so every one of these forms is a value you can actually compute: -(3/8), -3 / 8, and 3 / (-8) all come out to -0.375 -- the very same point on the number line. A negative fraction has ONE negative sign, and that sign can sit in three places: out in front, on the numerator, or on the denominator. Watch: -(3/8), -3/8, and 3/(-8) are all the same value. The rule is -(p/q) = (-p)/q = p/(-q). The trap is TWO negative signs: -3/(-8) has a negative on top AND bottom, and two negatives cancel, so -3/(-8) = 3/8, which is positive -- NOT equivalent to -(3/8).

canonical_error.pattern: Treats a fraction with negatives in two places as still negative, or thinks the three single-sign forms are different values
canonical_error.example: Says -3/(-8) is equivalent to -(3/8), or claims -3/8 and 3/(-8) are not the same
canonical_error.why: The student does not count the negative signs. One negative sign anywhere makes the fraction negative; two negative signs cancel to a positive.

skills.item_template: A negative fraction with several candidate forms; student selects all equivalent expressions (or the one that is NOT equivalent). MC/MS.

sample_items.stem: Select all options that are equivalent to -7/10.
sample_items.distractor_logic: The three single-negative forms equal -7/10. 7/10 has no negative; -7/(-10) has two negatives and equals +7/10.

sample_items.stem: Which expression is NOT equivalent to -(3/8)?
sample_items.distractor_logic: -3/(-8) has two negatives and equals +3/8. The others are single-negative forms of -3/8.

sample_items.stem: True or false: 5/(-9) has the same value as -5/9.
sample_items.distractor_logic: A negative on the denominator equals a negative on the numerator: both are -5/9.

sample_items.stem: A fraction has a negative sign on BOTH the numerator and the denominator. Is its value positive or negative?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Two negative signs cancel, so -a/(-b) = a/b, a positive value.

redirect_script.stop: How many negative signs are in that fraction?
redirect_script.prompt: Compute it as a division first: what decimal does that form actually land on? Count the negatives. ONE negative anywhere -- front, top, or bottom -- means the fraction is negative and all three match. TWO negatives cancel to positive. Check -3/(-8): that is two, so it is positive.
redirect_script.praise: You counted the signs and saw one negative can live in three equal places -- that's the identity.

vocabulary.definition: Different-looking expressions that have the exact same value.
The top number of a fraction.
The bottom number of a fraction.

worked_example_script.text: Write each form as a division and start computing decimals: -(2/5) is the opposite of 2/5, so -0.4. Now compute -2 / 5, then 2 / (-5), then -2 / (-5).
Use the division sign rule on each one: which forms land at -0.4 on the number line, and which one lands at +0.4?

-2 / 5 and 2 / (-5) each have one negative -- different signs, so both equal -0.4, the exact point where -(2/5) sits. But -2 / (-5) is same signs -- two negatives -- so it equals +0.4, a different point entirely.
Count the negative signs in each. Which ones are negative?
The first three each have one negative, so all equal -2/5. The last has two negatives, so it equals +2/5.
If a student groups -2/(-5) with the others, ask 'how many negatives cancel there?'
Your turn: which of -4/9, 4/(-9), -4/(-9) are equal to -(4/9)?

practice_problems.answer: Yes -- both have one negative sign, so both are -5/8.

practice_problems.answer: No. -(5/6) = 5/(-6); both equal -5/6. Moving one negative sign among front/top/bottom keeps the same value.

skills.name: Find the quotient of two signed integers
skills.i_do_script: Every division is a multiplication in reverse: -45 / 5 asks 'what number times 5 makes -45?' Only -9 works -- 9 x 5 would give +45. The multiplication facts you already trust are what set the sign. To divide two signed integers I do two things: divide the sizes, then decide the sign. The sign rule is the same as multiplication -- same signs give a positive, different signs give a negative. Watch: -45 / 5. Sizes: 45 / 5 = 9. Signs: negative and positive are different, so the answer is -9. Another: -72 / (-9). Sizes: 72 / 9 = 8. Signs are the same, so +8.

canonical_error.pattern: Divides the sizes correctly but attaches the wrong sign
canonical_error.example: For -45 / 5 writes 9 (ignoring the negative) or for -72 / (-9) writes -8 (stopping at one negative)
canonical_error.why: The student computes the magnitude but does not apply the same-signs/different-signs rule. Division inherits multiplication's sign behavior.

skills.item_template: A quotient of two integers with exactly one or two negatives. MC/numeric response.

sample_items.distractor_logic: 45/5 = 9; different signs -> -9. Ignoring the sign gives 9; subtracting gives -40.
36/4 = 9; different signs -> -9.
56/8 = 7; different signs -> -7. A near-miss fact gives -6.
72/9 = 8; same signs -> +8. Stopping at one negative gives -8.

redirect_script.stop: You have the number -- now what's the sign?
redirect_script.prompt: Turn it around: multiply your answer by the divisor -- do you land back on the starting number, sign and all? Split the job in two: divide the sizes, THEN apply the sign rule. Same signs make it positive, different signs make it negative. -45 / 5 is different signs, so the 9 becomes -9.
redirect_script.praise: You divided the sizes and then set the sign by the rule -- that's the whole move.

vocabulary.definition: The result of dividing one number by another.
A whole number or its negative: ..., -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, ...
Same signs give a positive quotient; different signs give a negative quotient.

worked_example_script.text: Division is a missing-factor question: -63 / (-7) asks 'what number times -7 gives -63?' Test both candidates: 9 x (-7) = ? And (-9) x (-7) = ?
9 x (-7) = -63 -- that hits the target. (-9) x (-7) = +63 -- wrong target. So -63 / (-7) must be +9: same signs come out positive because the multiplication check forces it.
Now -63 / 7 asks 'what number times 7 gives -63?' Which candidate works, 9 or -9?
What is 63 / 7? Now, are the signs the same or different in each?
63 / 7 = 9. -63 / (-7): same signs -> +9. -63 / 7: different signs -> -9.
If a student writes -63 / (-7) = -9, ask 'how many negatives, and do they cancel?'
Your turn: -40 / 8, then -54 / (-6).

practice_problems.answer: negative

practice_problems.notes: Different signs; baits leaving off the negative.

practice_problems.answer: The size is right (56/8 = 7), but the signs are different (negative divided by positive), so the quotient is -7. Priya dropped the negative sign.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: correct magnitude, wrong sign.

practice_problems.stem: Fill in the blank: -8 / ___ = 4. Explain the sign you chose.
practice_problems.answer: -2. You need a positive result, so the signs must match: -8 / (-2) = 4.
practice_problems.notes: Reverse: choose the divisor and justify its sign.

practice_problems.answer: -84 / (-12) is positive (same signs); 84 / (-12) is negative (different signs).
practice_problems.notes: Isolate the sign rule from the arithmetic.

skills.name: Calculate a quotient of rational numbers as a decimal
skills.i_do_script: Picture -12 / 5 as a $12 debt split evenly among 5 people: each share is still owed (negative) and sits between $2 and $3. An estimate like that catches a dropped sign or a wandering decimal point before the long division even starts. A fraction bar means divide, so to write a quotient as a decimal I actually divide the top by the bottom. Watch: -12 / 5. First the size: 12 / 5. Five goes into 12 twice with 2 left over; bring down a zero, 5 goes into 20 four times, so 2.4. Then the sign: different signs, so -2.4. If the division doesn't end, I round to the place the problem asks for.

canonical_error.pattern: Divides but attaches the wrong sign, or misplaces the decimal point
canonical_error.example: For -12 / 5 writes 2.4 (dropping the negative) or 0.24 (misplacing the decimal) instead of -2.4
canonical_error.why: The student either forgets to apply the sign rule to the decimal answer or loses track of place value during the division.

skills.item_template: A quotient of two rationals to be written as a terminating decimal (or rounded). Numeric response.

sample_items.stem: Calculate -12 / 5 as a decimal.
sample_items.distractor_logic: 12/5 = 2.4; different signs -> -2.4. Dropping the sign gives 2.4.

sample_items.distractor_logic: 9/4 = 2.25; different signs -> -2.25.

sample_items.stem: Calculate -3 / 8 as a decimal.
sample_items.distractor_logic: 3/8 = 0.375; different signs -> -0.375.

redirect_script.prompt: Estimate with the debt picture first: is each share owed or gained, and about how many dollars is it? A fraction bar means divide: carry out the division of the sizes, watching your place value. Then attach the sign by the same-signs/different-signs rule. -12 / 5 is different signs, so -2.4.
redirect_script.praise: You divided top by bottom and kept the right sign -- that's a decimal quotient.

skills.name: Divide fractions by multiplying by the reciprocal
skills.i_do_script: Dividing by a fraction asks a fitting question: how many of the second fraction fit inside the first? How many 2/3s fit in 5/6? Line up fraction bars: 5/6 covers the 2/3 bar once with a quarter of another copy left -- 5/4 copies fit. Multiplying by the reciprocal is exactly that count: every whole holds 3/2 copies of 2/3, so 5/6 of a whole holds 5/6 x 3/2 = 15/12 = 5/4 copies. THAT is why the flip works -- the reciprocal says how many copies each whole contains. Once the why is set, the shortcut is keep-change-flip: keep the first fraction, change divide to multiply, flip the second. (-2/5) / (3/4): keep -2/5, multiply by 4/3: -8/15. The sign rule rides on top -- one negative factor, so the answer is negative.

canonical_error.pattern: Multiplies straight across without flipping, or flips the wrong fraction
canonical_error.example: For (-2/5) / (3/4) writes (-2/5) x (3/4) = -6/20 (never flipped) or flips the first fraction instead of the second
canonical_error.why: The student skips the reciprocal step. Only the divisor (the second fraction) is flipped, and only after changing division to multiplication.

skills.item_template: A quotient of two signed fractions. Student multiplies by the reciprocal and reduces. MC/numeric response.

sample_items.distractor_logic: Flip the second: (-2/5)x(4/3) = -8/15. Multiplying straight across gives -6/20; flipping the wrong fraction gives -15/8.
(-3/4)x(-2/1) = 6/4 = 3/2; same signs -> positive. Multiplying straight across gives 3/8.
(1/2)x(-4/3) = -4/6 = -2/3; different signs -> negative.

redirect_script.stop: Did you flip the SECOND fraction?
redirect_script.prompt: Ask the fitting question first: how many of the second fraction fit in the first -- more than one copy or less? Then run the shortcut: keep the first fraction, change divide to multiply, flip ONLY the second fraction. (-2/5) / (3/4) becomes (-2/5) x (4/3). Does your answer's size match your fit estimate?
redirect_script.praise: You flipped the divisor and multiplied -- that's how you divide fractions.

vocabulary.definition: The fraction flipped over: the reciprocal of 3/4 is 4/3.
Keep the first fraction, change divide to multiply, flip the second fraction.

worked_example_script.text: Line up two fraction bars: 5/6 shaded on one, 2/3 shaded on the other. Dividing asks: how many of the 2/3 bar fit inside the 5/6 bar?
Does the 2/3 piece fit into 5/6 at least once? More than once? About how many copies fit?
One whole holds 3/2 copies of 2/3 -- that's what the reciprocal counts. So 5/6 holds 5/6 x 3/2 = 5/4 copies. Multiplying by the flip IS the fitting count.
What is the reciprocal of 2/3? Keep, change, flip -- what do you get?
(-5/6) x (3/2) = -15/12 = -5/4. One negative, so negative.
If a student writes (-5/6) x (2/3), ask 'which fraction do you flip -- the first or the second?'

practice_problems.stem: What is the reciprocal of 3/4?
Rewrite (2/5) / (3/4) as a multiplication.
Nadia divided (1/2) / (-3/4). Find and fix the mistake.
practice_problems.answer: Nadia forgot to flip the second fraction. Keep-change-flip gives (1/2) x (-4/3) = -4/6 = -2/3.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: multiplied straight across without the reciprocal.

practice_problems.stem: Explain why dividing by 1/2 makes a number bigger, using (3/4) / (1/2).
practice_problems.answer: Dividing by 1/2 multiplies by its reciprocal 2/1: (3/4) x 2 = 6/4 = 3/2, which is larger than 3/4.
practice_problems.notes: Reason about why the reciprocal step works.

activities.title: How Many Fit?
materials: Fraction strips or the fraction-bar printable
activities.instructions:
1. Give pairs 3 / (3/4). Before any symbols: lay 3/4 strips end to end along a 3-whole strip. How many fit? (4.)
2. Now compute 3 x 4/3 and compare. Why does multiplying by 4/3 give the same count? (Each whole holds 4/3 copies.)
3. Repeat with 1/2 / (3/4): the copy doesn't fit even once -- the answer must be less than 1. Confirm: 1/2 x 4/3 = 2/3 of a copy.
4. Debrief: write one sentence for the poster -- 'Dividing by a fraction counts how many fit; the reciprocal is the count per whole.'

activities.title: Divide, Then Match
activities.instructions:
1. Take a division card like (-5/6) / (2/3).
2. Rewrite it as keep-change-flip, multiply, and reduce.
3. Find the matching reduced-answer card.
4. The decoy cards are straight-across (unflipped) results -- avoid them.
5. Debrief: which decoys came from forgetting to flip?

activities.title: Flip the Second One
activities.instructions:
1. Read Nadia's work: (1/2) x (-3/4) = -3/8.
2. Circle the step where she should have flipped a fraction.
3. Redo it with keep-change-flip.
4. Write the three words of the rule and which fraction gets flipped.

content.error_step: Nadia multiplied straight across instead of flipping the divisor.

strategy_links.why: Thinking aloud 'keep, change, flip -- the SECOND one' models where the reciprocal goes.
The straight-across (unflipped) error is a precise find-and-fix target.
Fraction bars and area models make 'dividing by a fraction' concrete before the reciprocal shortcut.

questioning_prompts: Which fraction do you flip -- the first or the second?
What is the reciprocal of the divisor?
After you flip, is it multiply or divide?
How many negatives are there, so what sign is the answer?
Does your answer reduce?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student multiplies straight across without flipping, or flips the wrong fraction.
misconception_redirects.say: Keep-change-flip: keep the first fraction, change divide to multiply, and flip ONLY the second fraction to its reciprocal. Then multiply across and set the sign. (-2/5) / (3/4) becomes (-2/5) x (4/3).
misconception_redirects.praise: You flipped the divisor and multiplied -- that's how you divide fractions.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student flips correctly but forgets to reduce or mis-signs the product.
misconception_redirects.say: Finish the job: reduce the product to lowest terms and count the negatives to set the sign.
misconception_redirects.praise: You reduced and set the sign -- a complete fraction quotient.

quick_checks.look_for: 3/2 (flip to x(-2/1), two negatives -> positive). A -3/2 misses the double negative; +3/8 multiplied straight across without flipping (two negatives make the sign positive either way).
-8/15. An answer of -6/20 means the student multiplied straight across.

sentence_starters: Keep ___, change to multiply, flip ___ to ___.
There are ___ negative signs, so the quotient is ___.

Numerator times numerator, denominator times denominator.

skills.name: Solve real-world problems involving quotients of rational numbers
skills.i_do_script: Picture the diver's depth on a vertical number line: the trip starts at 0 and ends at -45 feet, cut into 5 equal one-minute drops. Each drop is a downward -- negative -- step, and that picture IS the problem. Real division problems ask 'how much per unit' or 'split into equal parts,' and the sign carries meaning. Watch: a diver goes down 45 feet over 5 minutes. Down is negative, so that is -45 / 5 = -9 feet per minute. The -9 tells me the diver drops 9 feet each minute. I set the sign from the situation -- down, loss, or below is negative -- then divide.

canonical_error.pattern: Assigns the wrong sign to the situation, or multiplies/adds instead of dividing
canonical_error.example: For 'down 45 feet over 5 minutes' writes 45 / 5 = 9 ft/min (missing the downward = negative) or 45 x 5
canonical_error.why: The student does not translate the direction word into a sign, or picks the wrong operation. A rate or an equal-share is a division, and down/loss/below is negative.

skills.item_template: A real-world rate or equal-share problem with a signed quantity. Student sets up the quotient, computes, and interprets. Numeric response (with units).

sample_items.stem: A diver descends 45 feet over 5 minutes at a steady rate. What is the diver's change in depth per minute?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Down is negative: -45 / 5 = -9. Missing the sign gives 9.

sample_items.stem: A bank account loses a total of $63 evenly over 9 months. What is the change per month?
sample_items.distractor_logic: -63 / 9 = -7; a loss is negative.

sample_items.stem: A stock falls $12.50 evenly over 5 days. What is the change per day?
sample_items.distractor_logic: -12.50 / 5 = -2.5; a fall is negative.

sample_items.stem: A recipe splits -3/4 cup of concentrate (a 3/4 cup reduction) equally among 3 batches. What is the change per batch?
The temperature dropped 15 degrees evenly over 6 hours. What was the change per hour, as a decimal?
sample_items.distractor_logic: -15 / 6 = -2.5; a drop is negative.

redirect_script.prompt: Sketch it first: where does the trip end on the number line -- above zero or below? First set the sign from the story: down, loss, or below is negative. This is a 'per unit' or 'equal share' question, so DIVIDE the total by the number of units. -45 / 5 = -9 feet per minute.
redirect_script.praise: You matched the direction to a sign and divided for the rate -- that's the application.

vocabulary.definition: How much of one quantity per one unit of another, found by dividing.
'For each,' signaling division (dollars per day, feet per minute).

worked_example_script.text: Sketch the submarine's depth: it starts at 0 at the surface and, 4 minutes later, sits at -60 m -- below the surface.
The trip down is cut into 4 equal minutes. Does the depth change by the same amount each minute? And is each of those one-minute changes upward or downward?
Four equal downward steps that total -60 means each minute is -60 / 4 = -15 m. An answer of +15 would mean the sub ROSE every minute -- and the picture says otherwise.
Write 'A submarine descends 60 m over 4 minutes. Change in depth per minute?'
Is 'descends' positive or negative? Is 'per minute' a divide?
Descends is negative and 'per minute' means divide: -60 / 4 = -15 m per minute.
If a student writes 15, ask 'which direction is the sub moving -- up or down?'
Your turn: a savings jar loses $18 evenly over 6 weeks -- change per week?

practice_problems.stem: 'Per hour' tells you to do which operation?
practice_problems.answer: Divide.

practice_problems.stem: A drop, a loss, or 'below' gets which sign?
practice_problems.answer: Negative.

practice_problems.stem: A diver descends 45 feet over 5 minutes. Change in depth per minute?
practice_problems.answer: -9 feet per minute

practice_problems.stem: A bank account loses $63 evenly over 9 months. Change per month?
practice_problems.answer: -$7 per month

practice_problems.stem: Sam found the per-day change of a stock that fell $12.50 over 5 days. Find and fix the mistake.
shown_work: Sam wrote: '12.50 / 5 = 2.50, so the change is +$2.50 per day.'
practice_problems.answer: A fall is negative, so the total change is -12.50 and -12.50 / 5 = -$2.50 per day. Sam used the right size but the wrong sign.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: missed that a fall is negative.

practice_problems.stem: The temperature dropped 15 degrees evenly over 6 hours. Change per hour, as a decimal?
practice_problems.answer: -2.5 degrees per hour

practice_problems.stem: A hiker's elevation changes by -1200 feet over 8 equal segments. What is the change per segment, and does it mean up or down?
practice_problems.answer: -1200 / 8 = -150 feet per segment; the negative means the hiker went DOWN 150 feet each segment.
practice_problems.notes: Interpret the sign of the quotient.

practice_problems.stem: Write a real-world story that the quotient -20 / 4 = -5 could represent.
practice_problems.answer: Sample: a pool drains 20 gallons evenly over 4 minutes, a change of -5 gallons per minute.
practice_problems.notes: Reverse: produce a context for a signed quotient.

activities.title: Story to Signed Quotient
activities.instructions:
1. For each story ('descends 45 ft over 5 min', 'loses $63 over 9 months'), choose the correct signed division set-up.
2. Compute the quotient and write its units.
3. Say what the sign means in the story (down, loss, below).
4. Debrief: which words told you the sign, and which told you to divide?

activities.title: Which Way Is the Change?
activities.instructions:
1. Read Sam's claim that a $12.50 fall over 5 days is +$2.50 per day.
2. Decide whether a 'fall' is positive or negative.
3. Redo the division with the correct sign.
4. Write which words in a story signal a negative amount.

content.worked_problem: Stock falls $12.50 over 5 days. Sam wrote 12.50 / 5 = +$2.50 per day.
content.error_step: Sam treated a fall as a positive change.
content.why: A fall is negative: -12.50 / 5 = -$2.50 per day.

strategy_links.why: Think-pair-share on 'is this change up or down?' builds interpretation of the quotient's sign.
A journal note mapping direction words to signs and to division consolidates the translation.
The wrong-sign-in-context error is precise and correctable with a find-and-fix.

questioning_prompts: Does this word (drop, loss, below) make the amount positive or negative?
Is this a 'per unit' or 'equal share' question -- so do you divide?
What total goes on top, and what number of units goes on the bottom?
What does the sign of your answer mean in the story?
What are the units of your quotient?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student assigns the wrong sign to the situation, or multiplies/adds instead of dividing.
misconception_redirects.say: First set the sign from the story: down, loss, or below is negative. This is a 'per unit' or 'equal share' question, so DIVIDE the total by the number of units. -45 / 5 = -9 feet per minute.
misconception_redirects.praise: You matched the direction to a sign and divided for the rate -- that's the application.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student gets the right number but leaves off the units or the meaning.
misconception_redirects.say: Finish the sentence: attach the units and say what the sign means -- '-9 feet per minute means dropping 9 feet each minute.'
misconception_redirects.praise: You interpreted the signed quotient back in the story.

quick_checks.prompt: A well's water level drops 24 inches evenly over 8 days. Change per day?
quick_checks.look_for: -3 inches per day. An answer of 3 misses that a drop is negative.

quick_checks.prompt: A debt of $30 is paid off evenly over 6 weeks (change from -30 to 0). Change per week?
quick_checks.look_for: +$5 per week (0 - (-30) = 30, then 30/6 = 5). A -5 misreads the direction of the change.

sentence_starters: '___' means the amount is ___, and 'per ___' means I divide.

worked_solution.stem: A diver descends 45 feet over 5 minutes at a steady rate. What is the diver's change in depth per minute?

steps.annotation: Translate the direction word into a sign.
A rate is a division.
Different signs give a negative quotient.

steps.math: -9 feet per minute (dropping 9 ft each minute)
steps.annotation: Interpret the sign in the story.

Split the total into equal months.

skills.name: Generate multiple equivalent forms of a negative fraction
skills.i_do_script: A rewrite is only 'equivalent' if it stays on the same spot on the number line -- and -(3/8) lives LEFT of zero, so every legal form must still be negative. One negative sign keeps it there; a second negative cancels the first and jumps the value across zero. Now I go the other direction: given a negative fraction, I generate several equal forms. The single negative sign can move to the front, the numerator, or the denominator. Watch: -(3/8). I can write -3/8 (sign on top) or 3/(-8) (sign on bottom). Both equal -(3/8). What I must NOT do is put a negative on both top and bottom, because -3/(-8) has two negatives and equals +3/8.

canonical_error.pattern: Generates a two-negative form as an 'equivalent,' or changes the value while rewriting
canonical_error.example: Lists -3/(-8) as equivalent to -(3/8), or writes -6/8 (changing the value) as a 'form' of -(3/8)
canonical_error.why: The student adds a second negative sign (which cancels to positive) or alters the numbers instead of just relocating the one negative sign.

skills.item_template: A negative fraction; student writes two or more equivalent forms (relocating the single negative sign). Numeric response.

sample_items.stem: Write two fractions equivalent to -(3/8).
sample_items.distractor_logic: Relocate the one negative sign: -3/8 (top) and 3/(-8) (bottom). Adding a second negative gives +3/8.

sample_items.stem: Write two fractions equivalent to -(5/9).
sample_items.distractor_logic: -5/9 and 5/(-9) both equal -(5/9).

sample_items.stem: Which expression is NOT a correct form of -(2/7): -2/7, 2/(-7), or -2/(-7)?
sample_items.distractor_logic: -2/(-7) has two negatives and equals +2/7.

sample_items.stem: Write -(4/11) with the negative sign on the denominator.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Move the single negative to the bottom: 4/(-11).

redirect_script.stop: Move the ONE sign -- don't add a second.
redirect_script.prompt: Check the spot: does your new form still land left of zero, or did it jump across? Keep exactly one negative sign and relocate it: front, numerator, or denominator. -(3/8) becomes -3/8 or 3/(-8). Putting a negative on both top and bottom makes it positive.
redirect_script.praise: You moved the single sign to make new equal forms -- that's fluent use of the identity.

vocabulary.definition: A fraction with the same value, here made by relocating the negative sign.
Not equal to zero -- the denominator can never be zero.

next_steps.if_pass: Ready for 8.NS and rational-number operations in equations.

worked_example_script.text: Mark where -(5/9) lives: a bit more than halfway from 0 toward -1, on the LEFT of zero. Every rewrite we make has to stay on that exact spot.
Move the one negative sign to the top: -5/9. Still left of zero? Now move it to the bottom: 5/(-9). A positive divided by a negative comes out ...?
Both rewrites keep exactly one negative, so both stay on the same spot left of zero. Add a SECOND negative, -5/(-9), and the two cancel -- the value jumps across zero to +5/9, a different number.
Write '-(5/9). Generate two equivalent forms.'
Where can the one negative sign go besides the front?
On the top: -5/9. On the bottom: 5/(-9). Both equal -(5/9).
If a student writes -5/(-9), ask 'how many negatives is that now, and what does it equal?'
Your turn: two forms of -(2/7).

practice_problems.stem: Write -(4/7) with the negative on the numerator.
Write -(4/7) with the negative on the denominator.
Write two fractions equivalent to -(3/8).
Write two fractions equivalent to -(5/9).
Jamie generated forms of -(2/7). Find and fix the mistake.
practice_problems.answer: 2/(-7) is correct, but -2/(-7) has two negatives and equals +2/7. A correct second form is -2/7. Jamie added a second negative sign.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: two-negative form treated as equivalent.

practice_problems.stem: Which is NOT equivalent to -(4/11): -4/11, 4/(-11), -4/(-11)?
Besides moving the sign, write a form of -(3/8) using equivalent fractions (scale up).
practice_problems.answer: Sample: -6/16 or 6/(-16); scale numerator and denominator by 2 and keep the single negative.
practice_problems.notes: Combine the sign identity with equivalent-fraction scaling.

practice_problems.stem: A classmate writes three 'equal' forms of -(5/6): -5/6, 5/(-6), and -5/(-6). Which one is wrong and why?
practice_problems.answer: -5/(-6) is wrong: two negative signs cancel to +5/6. The other two each have one negative and equal -(5/6).

activities.title: One Sign, Not Two
activities.instructions:
1. Read Jamie's forms of -(2/7): 2/(-7) and -2/(-7).
2. Count the negative signs in each.
3. Replace the wrong one with a correct single-negative form.
4. Write the rule for how many negatives a negative fraction may show.

content.error_step: Jamie's second form, -2/(-7), has two negative signs.
content.why: Two negatives cancel: -2/(-7) = +2/7. A correct form is -2/7.

activities.title: Three Places for One Sign
activities.instructions:
1. Flip a card such as -(3/8).
2. Each player writes two DIFFERENT equal forms by moving the single sign.
3. Score a point for each valid form; lose the point for any two-negative form.
4. Debrief: what are the only three legal places for the one negative sign?

strategy_links.why: Rapid choral generation of the three sign positions builds fluency with the identity.
The two-negative 'equivalent' is a precise error a find-and-fix corrects.
Journaling the three legal places for the sign consolidates the generalization.

questioning_prompts: Where are the three places the single negative sign can go?
How many negative signs should a negative fraction show?
What does a form with two negatives equal?
Did you keep the numbers the same and only move the sign?
Can you also make an equal form by scaling up?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student generates a two-negative form as an 'equivalent,' or changes the value while rewriting.
misconception_redirects.say: Keep exactly one negative sign and relocate it: front, numerator, or denominator. -(3/8) becomes -3/8 or 3/(-8). Putting a negative on both top and bottom makes it positive.
misconception_redirects.praise: You moved the single sign to make new equal forms -- that's fluent use of the identity.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student changes the numbers (e.g., -3/8 -> -4/8) thinking any rewrite counts.
misconception_redirects.say: To keep the same value, either move the ONE sign or scale top and bottom by the same factor -- don't change one number alone.
misconception_redirects.praise: You kept the value fixed while rewriting -- that's a true equivalent form.

quick_checks.look_for: -2/7 and 2/(-7). Any -2/(-7) diagnoses the double-negative error.
No -- it equals +5/6 (two negatives). 'Yes' misses the second sign.

sentence_starters: The one negative sign can go ___, ___, or ___.
-(p/q) equals ___ and ___, but NOT ___ because that has two negatives.

worked_solution.stem: Write two fractions equivalent to -(3/8), and name one form that is wrong.

steps.annotation: Keep exactly one negative sign.
Same value, sign relocated to the top.
Same value, sign relocated to the bottom.
A second negative sign flips it positive.

Relocate the sign to the top.

looking_back.label: Looking Back
looking_back.description: Skills the student should have but may need re-teaching.

diagnostic_flow.description: Start with S3 (calculate a quotient as a decimal) -- the At-proficiency computational engine and the clearest place the sign error surfaces. If they pass, move up to S4 (dividing fractions), S5 (real-world quotients), and S6 (generating equivalent forms). If they fail, drop to S2 (integer quotients and the sign rule) and S1 (the -(p/q) identity) to find where the sign understanding breaks. S4 doubles as a branch check on fraction division specifically.
